title: Frequency-Division Multiplexing in Magnonic Waveguides
authors: Alina-Cristina Bunea, Laurentiu Stoleriu, Giacomo Talmelli, Dan Neculoiu, Christoph Adelmann, Florin Ciubotaru
abstract: Frequency-division multiplexing is a key functionality for wave-based information processing, enabling multiple information channels to coexist within the same physical medium. Here, we experimentally investigate spin-wave multiplexing in a CoFeB waveguide using all-electrical excitation and detection. Two independently generated microwave signals are simultaneously coupled into the same spin-wave waveguide through inductive antennas and characterized using broadband vector network analyzer measurements. The transmission spectra obtained under single-channel and multiplexed operation exhibit excellent agreement, demonstrating that spin waves with different frequencies and wavelengths propagate simultaneously without measurable interaction in the linear regime. The observation is confirmed using both dual-sweep and sweep-plus-single-tone excitation schemes. A theoretical analysis based on linear superposition and phase-sensitive detection explains the absence of observable inter-channel interference for independent microwave sources. Micromagnetic simulations further confirm that the amplitudes and wavevectors of the individual spin-wave modes remain unchanged during co-propagation, demonstrating the absence of interaction over the entire propagation distance. The results provide direct experimental evidence that independent spin-wave channels can coexist in a single waveguide and support the implementation of frequency-division multiplexing in future magnonic computing and microwave signal-processing architectures.
summary: This paper experimentally proves that spin waves can be multiplexed using Frequency-Division Multiplexing (FDM) within a single magnetic waveguide. By measuring transmission spectra with multiple simultaneous microwave signals and confirming results via micromagnetic simulations, the authors establish that different frequency channels propagate independently without crosstalk. This work is crucial for advancing future magnonic computing and signal processing architectures.
main_problem: The research investigates the feasibility of Frequency-Division Multiplexing (FDM) for spin waves, aiming to enable multiple independent information channels within a single physical magnetic waveguide.
main_result: The authors experimentally and theoretically demonstrate that different frequency spin waves can coexist and propagate simultaneously in the linear regime without measurable interaction or crosstalk.
method: The study combines electrical characterization using Vector Network Analyzers (VNAs) for broadband measurements with theoretical analysis based on linear superposition and micromagnetic simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a CoFeB magnetic waveguide deposited on Si/SiO2, where spin waves are generated and detected electrically. The behavior is analyzed in the linear regime using established magnetodynamics principles.
key_observables: Transmission spectra ($S_{21}$), spin-wave power, complex transmission coefficients ($	ext{Re}/	ext{Im}(S_{21})$), spin-wave amplitude, and wavevectors as functions of frequency and propagation distance.
important_parameters: Applied magnetic field ($\mu_0H = 43 	ext{ mT}$); operation in the linear regime (low excitation power).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the validity of the superposition principle, assuming negligible nonlinear interactions between co-propagating modes.
figures_summary: Figures show device schematics and measurement setups using two VNAs. Key plots demonstrate that single-channel and multiplexed transmission spectra agree excellently, and simulations confirm unchanged mode amplitudes during co-propagation.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by introducing the FDM concept for magnonics, detailing the experimental setup involving dual-VNA measurements, presenting results showing non-interacting propagation, supporting these findings with theoretical linear superposition analysis, and finally confirming the robustness of the result via micromagnetic simulations.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum information processing, the demonstration of controlled wave coexistence in a solid-state system provides an excellent platform for studying linear wave coupling, energy transport, and non-interacting mode propagation—concepts relevant to open quantum systems modeling.
